whatItIs: A library of 14 book-derived "OBEY X" rule sets for coding agents, each shipped at three sizes (full / mini / nano) with a SKILL.md entrypoint, plus a private `_rule-workbench/` holding the compression, traceability and pairwise-compatibility instructions that produced them. 212 .md files, zero executable files in the repo (only .gitignore, LICENSE, and 14 `full.md` git symlinks at mode 120000).
method: The repo's real content is three long agent prompts in `_rule-workbench/`. PROCESS.md (195 lines) defines compression whose stated goal is output "decision-equivalent to the full source, not sentence-equivalent" (line 7): classify every source rule into one of eight labels (`default`, `book-thesis`, `decision-changing`, `micro-decision`, `conflict-resolver`, `trigger`, `checklist-only`, `framing`; lines 58-68), keep theses/decision-changers/conflict-resolvers in `mini.md`, keep only known-model-bias correctors in `nano.md`, and never drop a rule as a `default` without eval evidence because "Human-obvious is not the same as agent-default" (lines 181-183). Every surviving rule gets an `M*`/`N*` id in a per-book `traceability.md` citing the source section names and line ranges in `full.md`, and every source section must be dispositioned as `covered by Mx`, `covered by Nx`, or `intentionally lost` (lines 95-125). A "process bug vs book-specific miss" rule (lines 137-172) says that when a review finding belongs to a reusable class, edit PROCESS.md first and re-run the book, rather than hand-patching one output to reviewer taste. RELEASE.md (127 lines) fixes deterministic artifact metrics (`wc -l`, `wc -c`, Markdown list-item count) so the README matrix stays reproducible across releases. CHECK_COMPATIBILITY.md (613 lines) drives a 91-pair comparison of the `mini` files: a named high-risk pair list that may not default to "complementary", claim-level evidence rules forbidding whole-file citations, boilerplate rejection rules, three qualitative percentages (Conflict/Overlap/Complementarity), a disposable checkbox work queue processed strictly one pair at a time with resume, and explicit stop conditions. All 91 pair files exist and `docs/COMPATIBILITY.md` verdict counts (78 ✅ / 2 ❌ / 11 🔁) sum to 91, so the process was actually executed, not just written.
measures: Almost nothing, and it says so itself. docs/CRITICISM.md line 17 scores "There is no clear measurement of improvement" at validity 9/10 and "about 2/10 solved", conceding the repo "lacks evals, before/after task comparisons, defect-rate data, and review-time data". What it does measure is (a) its own artifacts — I reproduced the Clean Code README row exactly: 297 lines / 13851 B / 220 list items full, 47 / 3804 / 29 mini, 32 / 1235 / 14 nano — and (b) coverage of source sections by compressed rules, self-graded by the same model that wrote them. There is exactly one outcome experiment, README.md lines 183-201: two Codex refactors of one Ruby CLI (ciembor/vibe-coded-crap, 1 star, pushed 2026-05-13), one given the APoSD `mini` rules, the control given an AGENTS.md containing only the line `# OBEY A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout`; ChatGPT was then asked which code better implements the book and scored 74 vs 46. The objective half of that experiment found nothing: reek smells 1083 → 1077 (0.55%). The companion repo does contain a genuine rig — `quality_report.sh` (131 lines) and `measure_history.sh` (326 lines), which walks every commit in a detached worktree running rspec+simplecov+reek and emits measurements.csv/.jsonl — and it ran over 71 commits (reports/history-9213af1-2026-05-06_20-18-35/measurements.csv), but `coverage_percent` is empty in all 71 rows, so half the rig silently produced no data. The author states at README line 201 that deeper measurement is not planned. The compatibility percentages are declared "qualitative, not measured statistics" (CHECK_COMPATIBILITY.md line 331).
weaknesses: Provenance undermines the whole traceability edifice: the "books" were never read. docs/ADDING_THE_BOOK.md line 7 says "Ask the chatbot for the complete book outline", and docs/CRITICISM.md line 113 admits "it's a destilled content taken from ChatGPT". So the `full.md` that every `M*`/`N*` id traces back to with precise line ranges is itself an unverified model recollection — rigorous bookkeeping over an unaudited root. Second, ~90 pages of MUST-shaped process prose with zero executable checks: 212 .md files, no scripts, no CI, so "every section has a disposition" and "exactly 91 files" are verified by an agent reading its own output. Third, the one experiment is n=1, one project, one judge, a single free-form prompt, and the judge is a model from the same family that generated the rules; its objective control metric showed no effect. Fourth, false precision: single-percent scores that the spec itself calls non-statistical. Fifth, 78 of 91 pairs landed on ✅ despite a rule that forbids defaulting to ✅ — suspicious, but I read only 1 of the 91 files so I cannot call it. Finally, nothing here is about document readability; the subject matter is agent behaviour on code, so only the machinery transfers, not a line of content.

transferable.approach: Disposition ledger: after rewriting, every section of the original must be marked as surviving in rule X, merged into rule Y, or `intentionally lost` — never as "secondary" or "lower-yield". The spec explicitly bans vague omission labels (PROCESS.md lines 104-106).
transferable.whereItLives: ciembor/agent-rules-books, _rule-workbench/clean-code/traceability.md lines 70-93 ("Section coverage review"), spec at _rule-workbench/PROCESS.md lines 95-135
transferable.whyItMightWork: It is the one cheap, mechanical, falsifiable check in the repo: diff the original's section list against the ledger and any undispositioned section is a bug. terse's revise currently has no guard against quietly deleting a fact the reader needed; the audit catches that only if a reader question happens to cover it. I verified the ledger's citations are real: traceability.md M1 cites `Priority and behavior` (5-12) and `Hard rules` (290-297), and those exact line ranges in clean-code/clean-code.md are those headings' bodies.
transferable.collidesWith: revise's fourth pass (repair of measured failures). Adding a fifth bookkeeping pass risks exactly the failure terse already measured — "standards produce audits, not rewriting" — and this ledger is self-graded, the opposite of the reader ruler. Take it as a post-hoc assertion check on deletions only, not as a pass that shapes prose.

transferable.approach: Route each measured failure to either "method bug" or "this-document miss", with a hard rule that method bugs edit the method first and the document is re-run, and that post-review edits must be justified by source plus process, never by reviewer preference.
transferable.whereItLives: ciembor/agent-rules-books, _rule-workbench/PROCESS.md lines 137-172 ("Process vs Book Diagnosis") and line 193 ("Prefer re-running a book from a better process over manually sculpting the output after the fact")
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse's measurement chain produces the one thing this repo lacks — failures grounded in reader outcomes — but has nowhere to put a failure that will recur on the next document. This rule is the missing write-back path, and it is the only legitimate way terse's fixed writing rules could earn their content: a rule enters the list because a reader question failed in a class, not because a published standard said so.
transferable.collidesWith: revise pass 2, the fixed writing rules. They stop being fixed. That is the point, but it changes revise from a deterministic chain into a learning one, and it means two runs of revise on different repos can diverge — which breaks the reproducibility the 2026-09-10 bake-off relied on.

transferable.approach: Boilerplate rejection test as a validity filter on analysis output: a finding fails review if its sentence could be pasted unchanged into another document's report, if it cites a whole file instead of line ranges, or if it states a claim without interpreting why the cited line matters. The spec shows a bad/good citation pair.
transferable.whereItLives: ciembor/agent-rules-books, _rule-workbench/CHECK_COMPATIBILITY.md lines 286-321 ("Claim Evidence Rules", "Boilerplate Rejection Rules")
transferable.whyItMightWork: It is a cheap falsifiable test applied to an LLM's prose output, which is precisely the weak joint in terse: the audit's lie/placement/findability classification and the bake-off judges' rationales are both free-form model text with no validity check. Spot-checked and it works in practice — docs/compatibility/a-philosophy-of-software-design/clean-code.md cites clean-code.mini.md lines 16, 23 and 30-31, and those lines are exactly "keep functions small", "use comments only for rationale" and the split-phases/comment triggers it claims.
transferable.collidesWith: Nothing in terse; it tightens the judge and audit-classifier contracts rather than replacing them. Cost is one extra rejection round per finding.

transferable.approach: Never drop content as "the reader already knows this" without evidence from a reader run: the `default` label requires eval or known-failure evidence, and "Human-obvious is not the same as agent-default".
transferable.whyItMightWork: It is prove-don't-assert applied to deletion, and it is the exact inverse of terse's curse-of-knowledge pass: that pass adds back what the writer assumed known, this guard stops the rewriter from cutting what it assumes the reader knows. terse already has the evidence source this rule demands (the per-question reader seats), so the guard is enforceable here in a way it is not in that repo — where no eval exists and the label is therefore unusable by its own rule.
transferable.collidesWith: revise pass 3 (curse of knowledge), same subject from the opposite direction. Stating both could read as contradictory guidance to the rewriter unless one is framed as the add rule and the other as the delete gate.

transferable.approach: Cheapest possible control for an instruction bake-off: give the control arm only the name of the thing (a one-line AGENTS.md containing just `# OBEY A Philosophy of Software Design by John Ousterhout`) and the treatment arm the compressed rules, same model, same reasoning level, same plan-then-execute pipeline.
transferable.whereItLives: ciembor/agent-rules-books, README.md lines 184-199; branches ciembor/vibe-coded-crap @ aposd-refactor-mini-rules and @ aposd-refactor-no-rules
transferable.whyItMightWork: It is the same control shape terse used when five published standards lost to two unguided controls, run on the other side of the question (rules vs bare title) — and there the rules won on the judge. Recording it gives terse a precedent for the minimum viable control and a live example of judge-metric divergence: the judge called it 74 vs 46 while the objective count moved 1083 to 1077. That divergence is the argument for terse's reader-question ruler over any single-judge rating.
transferable.collidesWith: Nothing to replace; it is a precedent for the bake-off's control design, and a caution that a single free-form judge rating is not a measurement.
